Case studies

Illustrative examples, not customer references

The examples below are fictional composites built to show our method. They are labelled as illustrative because they do not describe named clients. Figures are indicative and exist to show the shape of the outcomes we design for.

Discuss a similar situation

Illustrative Example 01

Payments

Alert triage backlog at a payments institution

  • AML
  • Case management
  • QA sampling

Situation

A UK-regulated payments institution processing several million transactions a month had built its alert review process across a shared spreadsheet, a case tool and email. Alert volumes had grown after a product expansion, and the review queue was measured in weeks rather than days.

Problem

Analysts prioritised alerts by instinct. Duplicate alerts were reviewed separately, quality assurance sampled randomly after closure, and the reasoning behind dispositions was often recorded in free text that was hard to retrieve. Senior managers could not see which alerts were aging or why.

Approach

We ran a four-week discovery to map the real alert journey, identify duplicate generation patterns and quantify rework. We then redesigned triage around risk-based queues, with the rules for queue assignment set and approved by the MLRO function.

Workflow design

A single case record per customer and risk theme replaced per-alert tracking. Stages were defined with service levels, mandatory disposition fields and a rationale standard. QA moved from post-closure random sampling to risk-weighted sampling at the point of disposition.

Automation design

Alerts were clustered by customer and typology before reaching analysts. Document and transaction summaries were drafted automatically for each case, with the analyst editing and approving the summary before it became part of the record. All draft and final versions were logged.

Outcomes

The queue was brought within the internal service level within two quarters. The QA team gained a view of defect patterns by analyst and typology, which led to targeted training. Supervisory information became available on demand from the case record.

42%Reduction in median time to disposition (illustrative)
31%Fewer duplicate alerts reaching analysts (illustrative)
100%Dispositions with a recorded rationale (illustrative)

Illustrative Example 02

Financial services

Periodic KYC refresh for a challenger bank

  • KYC
  • Refresh cycles
  • Document workflows

Situation

A challenger bank had onboarded a large retail customer base quickly and was now facing a backlog of periodic reviews. Refresh schedules were held in a data extract that was updated manually each month.

Problem

Review tasks were allocated unevenly, documents arrived through several channels, and the completion record for each refresh was split between the customer file and an operations tracker. The bank could not evidence timely reviews for higher-risk segments.

Approach

We designed a risk-segmented refresh model with defined cadences and decision authorities, then built the operational workflow around it. The change was phased by customer segment to keep the backlog under control.

Workflow design

Refresh tasks were generated automatically from risk rating and last review date. Customers received a controlled document request with a checklist. Each stage captured who acted, what was checked and what decision was taken, with escalation to a senior reviewer where the risk rating required it.

Automation design

Document receipt triggered automatic classification and completeness checks. Documents that failed checks were routed to a verification queue with the specific gap identified. Reminder and escalation messages followed the approved template set.

Outcomes

Higher-risk reviews became timely and measurable. The bank could show a completion record for each refresh that matched the risk-based policy, and the backlog was cleared in a phased plan agreed with the regulator through the normal supervisory dialogue.

3 monthsTime to clear the legacy review backlog (illustrative)
60%Reduction in manual document chasing (illustrative)
100%Higher-risk reviews on schedule after phase two (illustrative)

Illustrative Example 03

Asset and wealth management

Third-party governance for an investment platform

  • Vendor governance
  • Due diligence
  • Issue management

Situation

An investment platform used more than forty third-party providers across administration, data, custody support and technology. Due diligence was completed at onboarding, and periodic reviews were tracked in spreadsheets maintained by different teams.

Problem

Nobody held a complete view of provider risk. Issues raised during reviews were tracked in email and rarely closed. Contract renewal dates were missed, and the evidence for provider oversight was not available in a form the risk committee could use.

Approach

We mapped providers by criticality and data access, then designed a governance model with differentiated review cycles. The operational workflow was built to make the right review happen at the right time with a named owner.

Workflow design

Each provider record linked to its services, data flows, contract terms and risk rating. Review cycles were scheduled by criticality. Findings created actions with owners and due dates, and actions that passed their due date escalated automatically to the relevant committee.

Automation design

Questionnaire responses were ingested and summarised against the risk framework, with the reviewer confirming the summary. Contract renewal alerts were generated from the record, and performance data from providers was collected through a standard template.

Outcomes

The risk committee received a single, current view of provider risk each quarter. Overdue actions reduced sharply once escalation was automatic, and the team spent less time chasing responses.

40+Providers under a single governance model (illustrative)
80%Reduction in overdue review actions (illustrative)
QuarterlyCommittee reporting from a single record (illustrative)

Illustrative Example 04

Consumer lending

Regulatory return assembly for a RegTech-supported lender

  • Regulatory reporting
  • Reconciliation
  • Sign-off controls

Situation

A specialist consumer lender prepared its periodic regulatory returns from several source systems. Each cycle required a small team to extract data, reconcile it manually and assemble the return in a shared workbook over several days.

Problem

Reconciliations were performed by individuals with no shared control standard. Late corrections were applied directly in the workbook, and there was no reliable record of which adjustments had been made or approved.

Approach

We documented the return logic, identified the control totals that should reconcile each cycle, and designed a controlled assembly process with explicit sign-off points. Data owners were engaged to fix the source issues that drove most exceptions.

Workflow design

Source data was loaded into a controlled environment and reconciled against control totals before assembly began. Exceptions were raised to named data owners. The preparer, reviewer and senior approver each signed off in sequence, and any post-submission correction followed a defined amendment route.

Automation design

Extraction and reconciliation checks were automated, with reconciliation breaks listed by owner. Submission packs were generated from the approved data set, and the full version history was retained with the return.

Outcomes

The assembly cycle moved from several days to a fraction of that time, and the sign-off trail for each return could be produced on request. The number of late adjustments fell because most exceptions were resolved at source.

70%Reduction in assembly effort per cycle (illustrative)
0Unapproved adjustments in the final two cycles (illustrative)
3 daysSaved from each reporting cycle (illustrative)

Illustrative Example 05

Asset management

Control evidence management for an asset manager

  • Compliance operations
  • Evidence
  • Audit readiness

Situation

An asset manager operating across several fund ranges maintained a control library of around two hundred controls. Evidence for each control was collected by the owning teams at different times, and external audit requests arrived with short deadlines.

Problem

Evidence was often reconstructed rather than retrieved. Control owners disagreed on what evidence was required, and the audit preparation team spent weeks each year assembling packs from email and shared drives.

Approach

We aligned the control library to the evidence each control should generate, agreed the evidence standard with internal audit, and designed the collection workflow so that evidence was captured as controls operated.

Workflow design

Each control record stated its frequency, owner, evidence type and test method. Evidence submissions were time-stamped and linked to the control. Missed submissions triggered reminders and escalation to the control owner’s manager.

Automation design

Evidence requests were generated from the control calendar. Submissions were checked for completeness against the evidence standard. Audit packs were produced from the record by filter, with an index for the auditor.

Outcomes

Audit preparation moved from a seasonal project to a monthly review. Internal audit reported fewer evidence exceptions, and control owners spent less time responding to ad hoc requests.

200Controls with defined evidence standards (illustrative)
75%Reduction in audit preparation time (illustrative)
90%Evidence submitted on time after escalation design (illustrative)

Illustrative Example 06

Consumer lending

AI-assisted adverse media review for a consumer lender

  • AI governance
  • Screening
  • Human-in-the-loop

Situation

A consumer lender wanted to reduce the time analysts spent reviewing adverse media hits during onboarding. An initial pilot had been run by an innovation team without a governance framework, and the risk function had not approved its continuation.

Problem

The pilot produced summaries that analysts trusted without checking, and there was no record of which summaries had been relied on. The use case had no owner, no risk tier and no monitoring for error rates.

Approach

We reset the use case within an AI governance framework. We assessed the risk, set the oversight model, defined the review standard and built the monitoring. The pilot was paused until the controls were in place, then restarted in a controlled form.

Workflow design

Adverse media results were summarised for each hit with source links. Analysts recorded a disposition for each hit, and the summary was marked as accepted, edited or rejected. Low-confidence summaries were routed to a senior reviewer automatically.

Automation design

The summarisation step ran behind an approval gate with the model version and prompt set recorded for each output. Monthly sampling compared analyst dispositions with the summaries to measure reliance and error rates.

Outcomes

The risk function approved the use case as Tier 2 with defined sampling. Analysts saved time on routine hits while complex matches received fuller review. The use case became the reference pattern for the firm’s AI register.

35%Reduction in review time for routine hits (illustrative)
4%Sampled summaries requiring material correction, trending down (illustrative)
100%Outputs traceable to model version and reviewer (illustrative)
